doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: The pull of live drum music and the drum's spiritual power
summary: Rowe asks why live drumming draws people in; Cascadu speaks of the drum membrane, Trinidad's drum culture, and the drummers who inspired him.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I mean, well, I want to talk about you and your band mates, the thing you did yesterday was — when I asked a question I said, “My head is spinning.” And it was really true. Because there’s something about, this is not a question but rather an observation and maybe you can talk about it. There’s something about this percussion rhythms and things that you gentlemen played that reaches so deep into you — I don’t know what it is, but — like if you were in New York City and you were walking and all of a sudden you heard this and you could tell well that’s live drum music, like you would go there. It’s like a magnet or something. What is that about?

I think the drum has the ability to reach deeply into your soul. That’s the power of that vibrating membrane and that piece of wood. It has the power to call you. And there’s something spiritually that we respond to, that people respond to, just like you’re saying you know. You hear these drums and there’s something that you want to go and visit it. You want to be in the presence of that. And I think it’s a very primal call to the deepest part of our being. Because we’re all connected to that somehow or the other you know. I mean philosophically okay you know this is a membrane, a form, you know there’s a membrane vibrating here. We come through a membrane into life you know. That, it is a membrane that beats in the womb. We are surrounded by that membrane. So somehow or the other we are connected both biologically, from the time of our creation, the time of intention to this membrane of some kind of link, some kind of spiritual link from where we came from. And the drum has access, or the drum reminds us of that connection, of

that place where we come from. Monk, I’ve seen, in Trinidad, there are people, and we have a very, very strong drum culture in Trinidad. And I have been to concerts in these big halls, You know people come in all — their suits, all suited up, and we come, we are a British colony for over 150 years, a Spanish colony for over 300 years etcetera. You know? And you know people will speak and dress in a very European way. And that drum would play in that concert hall. And people would start to, you know, dressed up in their fine fancy you know. And there’s something very, very primal that we relate to with the drum. And those of us who play and who dedicate our lives to this, like I was talking about people like Don Alias and Emile Latimer who were amazing inspirations for me, Montego Joe, Chief Bey, all these guys, man, who were like the forerunners, and then in Trinidad there was a drummer by the name of Andrew Beddoe. I mean when he played you were transported to another place altogether. In Haiti Tiroro, man this guy, the talking about Tiroro is that his hands were a phenomenon. And what he did with his hands could not be consciously analyzed at all. What came out of the meeting between his hands and the skin was from another world altogether, and it was he, Tiroro, was one of the guys who inspired Don Alias as well as Emile Latimer because Emile always taught me, Emile always said to me man you really want to listen to the drummer, if you really want to play, go check out Tiroro. You know? Check out his music. So I think that aspect of playing percussion, of being close to sounds that come from nature — because that’s what we do. We color the music with, you know, with membranes, with pods, with seeds, with conch horns you know, with animal horns and shells and all. That’s what we do. We’re very organic. So the entire percussive world as we know it, traditionally, right — and what do the shamans use when they are trying to heal people and go into that spiritual realm? They use seeds. They use the membrane of an animal. The Native Americans used the drum you know [scats]. Right? I mean the rattle you know, the maraca or the rattle or the shaker or whatever you call it, all of these instruments help us to transcend the physical and access the metaphysical. Help us to leave the mundane and get to the spiritual. So when — you are absolutely right — what is this thing that makes you — that draws you in? It’s because something is happening that causes you to deeply, spiritually, to come and be present.

I didn’t even introduce you on film. This is Cascadú. And I can’t imagine that you ever play a gig where you are coasting. And by that I mean those of us who play gigs all the time, sometimes you’re playing and you know it’s just, you’re looking at your watch and oh man it’s only 8:15 and — when I was watching the three of you yesterday it’s hard for me to imagine that you would do that.
